# RULE EXTRACTION: Competing Demands for Water & Statutory Priority

---

## PRIMARY INSTRUMENTS

### 1. Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act 522) — Section 12 [verbatim]

"The property in and control of all water resources is vested in the President on behalf of, and in trust for the people of Ghana" [verbatim]

**Effect:** Water is held in trust for the people; no entity has ownership; all water use requires reference to WRC.

---

### 2. Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692) — Regulation 7 (Priority of water use) [verbatim]

"(1) In considering an application, the Commission shall be guided by (a) the prevailing water policy, (b) domestic water use, and (c) any other water use which fulfils the goals of national socio-economic development. (2) Where the priorities of two applications are the same, the first in time shall be given the priority" [verbatim]

**Effect:** Explicit statutory hierarchy: domestic use is the primary guiding criterion; socio-economic development uses are secondary; temporal priority applies where uses rank equally.

---

### 3. Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692) — Regulation 4 (Review criteria) [verbatim]

The materials reviewed set out that the WRC must review applications to ascertain that "the proposed water use is in accordance with the national water use policies and plans and will not cause irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment" [verbatim].

The WRC must also hold "a public hearing in cases where a) there is adverse public reaction to the proposed use, b) the proposed use involves the dislocation, relocation and resettlement of people, or c) the WRC considers that the proposed use will have a negative impact on the natural resources of a basin" [verbatim]

**Effect:** WRC must refuse or condition permits that cause irreparable harm to water resources, public health or the environment; public hearing required where basin-wide negative impact is likely.

---

### 4. Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703) — Section 17 [verbatim via secondary source]

The mineral rights holder must obtain "the requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission before it may '…obtain, divert, impound, convey and use water from a river, stream, underground reservoir or watercourse within the land the subject of the mineral right'" [verbatim]

**Effect:** Mineral right is NOT a standalone entitlement to water; separate WRC approval is mandatory.

---

### 5. Water Charter for the Volta River Basin, December 2018 — Article 10 (Relations between types of use) [verbatim]

"Among all the different types of water use in the Basin, no particular use shall be given priority over the others. However, should competing uses of water prevent all the requirements from being met, special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings." [verbatim]

**Effect:** Equal standing in principle; but where water scarcity forces choice, basic human needs (domestic, drinking, sanitation) take precedence.

---

## SECONDARY AUTHORITY (INTERPRETIVE GLOSS)

### Statutory Integration & WRC Decision-Making Duty

Ainuson argues (Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.28–39) that the customary law rules on water use have been supplanted by statutory law under the Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act 522), which now governs ownership, use and management of water resources. 

Critically, Ainuson documents that the management of water use in mineral operations is based on an integrative approach which imposes an obligation on a number of government agencies, and that the WRC representative sits on the Minerals Commission's standing technical committee; when a mineral application is submitted, the WRC representative advises the committee as to the effect of proposed operations on water bodies in and around the mining area. 

Significantly, if the proposed mining operation will adversely affect water resources for which there can be no appreciable remedial action to reduce or minimize the adverse effect, the Minerals Commission may advise the Minister to exercise his/her power under section 4 of the Minerals and Mining Act to set the land aside from mining for being an ecological fragile area.

### Balancing Competing Uses

Ainuson further notes (p.24–25) that the mining industry can exist and continue to grow if the regulatory regime can strike a fair balance between the mining industry's effect on water use and the ability of the rest of the society to use water, and that the beginning of the conversation as to striking a fair balance between the competing uses for water is the process of acquiring water rights in mineral operations.

Williams et al. argue (Water Implications of Large-Scale Land Acquisitions in Ghana — Williams, T.O. et al. — p.10–16) that while operational rules and procedures for water governance appear adequate for rational decision-making, their usefulness is limited because they are divorced from land acquisition procedures and only come into play after land has been acquired and production activities are about to start. They emphasize that the potential impacts on livelihoods and water rights of existing land users were not discussed at all in the cases reviewed, pointing to a systemic failure to protect downstream users in permit decisions.

### IWRM Principles

Owusu et al. characterize (A review of Ghana's water resource management and the future prospect — Owusu et al. — p.8–9) the WRC's adoption of Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) as a good decision, and note that as IWRM stresses the significance of involving all stakeholders—authorities, organizations, the public and private sectors, non-state actors and civil society—in the management of water resources, Ghana is doing same with the WRC decentralizing its roles by the generation of boards in the various major basins in the country.

---

## SYNTHESIS: STATUTORY HIERARCHY & CRITICAL GAPS

**Explicit Priority Rule (Regulation 7, L.I. 1692):**
- **First tier:** Domestic water use (drinking, sanitation, household)
- **Second tier:** Water uses fulfilling national socio-economic development goals (which may include mining, agriculture, industrial supply)
- **Temporal rule:** Where priorities rank equally, first-in-time prevails

**Irreparable Harm Standard (Regulation 4, L.I. 1692):**
- WRC must refuse or condition permits that cause "irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment"
- WRC must hold public hearing if proposed use will have negative impact on basin's natural resources

**No Standalone Mining Entitlement (Act 703, s.17):**
- Mineral right does NOT confer independent right to abstract water
- Separate WRC water permit is mandatory precondition

**Trust Duty (Act 522, s.12):**
- Water held in trust for the people of Ghana
- Not for exclusive benefit of any sector

**Basin-Level Principle (Water Charter, Article 10):**
- No use has automatic priority
- Where scarcity forces choice, basic human needs take precedence

---

## CRITICAL INTERPRETIVE ISSUE — NOT EXPRESSLY RESOLVED

⚠ **NOT FULLY ADDRESSED IN RETRIEVED MATERIALS:**

The materials reviewed do not expressly define whether **"irreparable damage"** (the operative standard) encompasses:
- Reduction in downstream dry-season flows below levels needed for existing users' established practices
- Cumulative water loss to public utilities (Ghana Water Company) serving district capitals  
- Environmental flow requirements to sustain aquatic ecosystems and fisheries

Similarly, the materials do not explicitly state whether **"basic human needs"** (Article 10, Water Charter) extends to:
- Protecting the water entitlements of downstream farmers who predate the mining lease
- Safeguarding the public utility's supply obligations to urban consumers

The WRC's discretionary weighing process under Regulation 7 is implicit: the statute requires consideration of "domestic use" and "socio-economic development," but does not algorithmically resolve a conflict where mining (a development use) threatens domestic supplies (the priority use).

**【FILL: The text of Ghana's National Water Policy (2007) or any WRC guidance document on allocation hierarchy in conflict scenarios — to establish whether WRC has published operational criteria for resolving Regulation 7 tiers when both domestic AND development uses compete for the same source. Official source: WRC Ghana website or Ministry of Water Resources repository.】**

# RULE EXTRACTION — Applicable Permits, Approvals and Regulatory Processes for Mining Operations Using Water in Ghana

## Primary Operative Provisions

### (a) Water-Use Permit Requirement from Water Resources Commission

"the holder of a mineral right must obtain the requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission before it may '… obtain, divert, impound, convey and use water from a river, stream, underground reservoir or watercourse within the land the subject of the mineral right'" — Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), section 17 [verbatim, quoted via Ainuson]

**Water Use Permit Application and Procedural Requirements:**

- "a person may obtain a permit from the Commission for: (a) domestic water use (b) commercial water use, (c) municipal water use, (d) industrial water use, (e) agricultural water use, (f) power generation water use, (g) water transportation water use, (h) fisheries (aquaculture) water use (i) environmental water use (j) recreational water use, and (k) under water (wood) harvesting." — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 1 [verbatim]

- **Application and publication:** "An applicant for a permit shall file the application form with the Commission… The applicant shall obtain an application form as specified in Schedule A for completion from the Commission" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 2(1)–(2) [verbatim]

- **Gazette and newspaper publication before grant:** "The Commission shall prior to making a grant of a permit, publish in the Gazette and in at least one national newspaper a notice (a) stating the purpose of the application, and (b) inviting objections from the public to be submitted to the Commission within three months from the date of the first publication" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 3(1) [verbatim]

- **Commission's investigation and decision:** "The Commission shall in considering an application, conduct an investigation to ascertain whether the proposed use of the water (a) is in accordance with the established water use policies and plans, and (b) will not cause irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 5(1) [verbatim]

- **Mandatory public hearing in defined circumstances:** "The Commission shall hold a public hearing in respect of an application where (a) upon a notice issued under regulation 3(1) there is adverse public reaction to the proposed use; (b) the use of the water involves the dislocation, relocation, resettlement or in any manner cause the destruction of the natural water resources of the community" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 6(1)(a)–(b) [verbatim]

- **Grant and conditions:** "the Commission shall grant a permit to an applicant who satisfies the requirements of these Regulations… Where the Commission has reasons based on (a) technical data, (b) sustainability of the water resources, (c) national security, (d) public safety, or (e) other reasonably justification the Commission shall refuse to grant the permit to the applicant" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 13(1)–(2) [verbatim]

- **Parliamentary ratification:** "Unless otherwise stated, a permit granted by the Commission shall be subject to ratification by Parliament" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 13(5) [verbatim]

---

### (b) Environmental Permit/Approval from Environmental Protection Agency

"Prior to undertaking mineral operations, the holder of mineral rights is also required to obtain permission from the Forestry Commission as well as obtain an environmental permit from the Environmental Protection Agency." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 36 [secondary analysis of statutory requirements]

**EPA Authority to Require Environmental Impact Assessment:**

"Under section 12 of the Environmental Protection Agency Act, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) may by notice in writing require any mining operations which in the opinion of EPA has or is likely to have adverse effect on the environment to submit to the EPA an environmental impact" [statement; continuation of quote in original expected to read "statement" or similar; passage truncated] — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 38

---

### (c) Environmental Impact Assessment and Environmental Management Plan Requirements

**EIA Required Where WRC and EPA Agree It Is Necessary:**

"Where the Commission in consultation with the Environmental Protection Agency considers a proposed water use to constitute a use which requires an environmental impact assessment, the applicant shall attach to the application evidence that an environmental impact assessment has been approved by the Environmental Protection Agency." — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 12(1) [verbatim]

**EPA-Mandated Environmental Management Plan as Condition of Water Permit:**

"Where in the opinion of the Environmental Protection Agency the proposed or existing water use requires an environmental management plan, that requirement shall be one of the conditions for the grant of water use permit." — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 12(2) [verbatim]

---

### (d) Forestry Commission Permit (If Applicable)

"the holder of mineral rights is also required to obtain permission from the Forestry Commission as well as obtain an environmental permit from the Environmental Protection Agency." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 36 [secondary; pinpoints Forestry Commission Act 1999 (Act 571), section 2 as the authority]

---

### (e) Relationship, Sequencing and Integration of Permitting Processes

**Statutory Integration via Minerals Commission Standing Committee:**

"within the Minerals Commission there is a standing technical committee that is constituted to consider applications for mineral rights before the Minerals Commission makes a recommendation to the Minister in charge of minerals to issue a license for the exercise of mineral rights." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 38

**Composition and Function of the Standing Committee:**

"The standing committee in recognition of the symbiotic nature of mineral exploitation has as part of its members a representative from the Water Resources Commission, Forestry Commission, Lands Commission, Geological Services Department and the Environmental Protection Agency. Therefore, when an application is submitted to the Minerals Commission for processing, the Minerals Commission will take the views of the representatives of the other agencies with respect to the technical competency of the application as it affects their respective agency's scope of work." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 39

**WRC Representative's Role in Assessing Water Impacts:**

"the representative of the Water Resources Commission is able to advice the committee as to the effect of the proposed mineral operations on water bodies in and around the mining area." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 39

**Conditional Grant of Mineral Right Linked to Water-Use License Requirement:**

"if by the nature of the application the applicant must obtain a water use license the Water Resources Commission can indicate such requirement so that the grant of the mineral right by the Minister will be subject to a water use license obtained from the Water Resources Commission." — Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson, p. 39

**Parallel EPA–WRC Collaboration on EIA and Environmental Management Plan:**

"The EPA and the WRC are expected to collaborate when a proposed water use requires an EIA and when the proposed or existing water use requires an environmental management plan. In each case, a water permit will not be issued unless evidence that the necessary requirement has been met is produced and attached to the water permit application." — Water Implications of Large-Scale Land Acquisitions in Ghana — Williams, T.O.; Gyampoh, B.; Kizito, F. and Namara, R., Water Alternatives, p. 11

---

### (f) Public Participation and Objection Procedures

**Public Notice and Objection Period (3 months):**

"The Commission shall prior to making a grant of a permit, publish in the Gazette and in at least one national newspaper a notice (a) stating the purpose of the application, and (b) inviting objections from the public to be submitted to the Commission within three months from the date of the first publication" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 3(1) [verbatim]

**Formal Objection Resolution by Water Users Committee:**

"Where (a) a person claims water right or other interest in a water resource which is the subject of a new application, or (b) conflicting claims of interest are made over the same water resources, the claim shall be referred by the Commission to the Water Users Committee of the Commission for resolution. The Committee shall consider all statements from the parties and any information supporting the claims of the parties. The proceedings of the Committee shall be informal and shall be governed by the rules of natural justice. The Committee shall submit its report and recommendations to the Commission within fourteen days after completion of the hearing." — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 8(1)–(4) [verbatim]

**Public Hearing Mandatory in Certain Circumstances:**

"The Commission shall hold a public hearing in respect of an application where (a) upon a notice issued under regulation 3(1) there is adverse public reaction to the proposed use; (b) the use of the water involves the dislocation, relocation, resettlement or in any manner cause the destruction of the natural water resources of the community" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 6(1)(a)–(b) [verbatim]

**Commission Collaboration with Traditional Authorities and Other Agencies in Public Hearing:**

"For the purposes of conducting a public hearing, the Commission shall collaborate with (a) the Environmental Protection Agency (b) the traditional authorities of the community and (c) the relevant government institutions and agencies" — Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 6(2) [verbatim]

---

## Summary of Permitting Architecture

⚠ **The complete text of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), sections 17 and 35, and the Environmental Protection Agency Act, 1994 (Act 490), section 12, are not in their full operative form in the materials — confirm the exact statutory language against the official texts.**

The rule establishes that mining operations requiring water use are subject to **sequential and integrated permitting**: (1) a water-use permit from the WRC under the Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), which requires publication, public objection procedures, investigation into sustainability and irreparable damage, and mandatory public hearing in defined circumstances; (2) an environmental permit from the EPA, potentially including an EIA requirement and environmental management plan as a condition of the WRC water permit; (3) a Forestry Commission permit if operations occur in forested areas; and (4) an integrative review via the Minerals Commission standing committee (composed of WRC, EPA, Forestry Commission, and other agencies) which may condition the grant of the mineral right itself on satisfaction of water-use licensing. The WRC water-permit regime is NOT displaced by a prior mineral right grant — it operates as a separate and binding regulatory requirement, triggered where the proposed operations "use water in its natural state and/or affect water resources."
